{"type":"finish","output":"Detailed Technical Analysis of the DSH Queue Incident (09:00-10:00)

Using only the synthetic evidence E01-E10, the incident is best characterized as a dependency-induced backpressure event rather than a compute-capacity shortage. At 09:00 the system was healthy: queue depth was 120 with 8 workers, median latency 1.8s, and CPU/memory/disk at 43/51/22% (E01, E04). Between 09:10 and 09:14 the queue exploded from 120 to 1,850 while worker count stayed at 8, and median latency climbed to 14.2s (E02, E03). Crucially, at 09:15 dependency B began returning HTTP 429 for 31% of requests (E05). This temporal ordering strongly implicates dependency B rate-limiting as the primary cause: the resource metrics never indicated saturation, so workers were idle-waiting on a throttled upstream rather than CPU/memory bound.

The retry policy acted as a major amplifier. At 09:16 retry volume increased 420% under exponential backoff capped at three retries (E06). Because retries re-enter the queue against the same throttled dependency, they multiplied load without improving success, deepening the backlog. This is confirmed by E08: disabling retries for dependency B dropped queue depth 38% in six minutes, albeit with a higher direct failure rate. Thus retries converted transient throttling into a self-sustaining queue storm.

Adding workers had limited effect because the bottleneck was external, not internal. E07 shows raising workers 8->16 reduced queue depth only 6% over ten minutes. With dependency B returning 429 for ~31% of calls, extra workers mostly blocked on the same limited outbound budget; more concurrency against a fixed rate limit yields marginal throughput gain and can worsen throttling. Hence scaling workers was an ineffective lever for a dependency-constrained incident.

Primary cause vs amplifiers: Primary cause = dependency B rate-limit enforcement beginning ~09:15 (E05). Amplifiers = (a) the retry storm (E06), (b) insufficient worker utilization due to external blocking, and (c) the reactive worker scaling that did not address the root (E07). The clean resolution in E09, where raising B rate limits drove 429 below 1% and queue below 150 in eleven minutes, corroborates the dependency-centric diagnosis and rules out internal capacity as root.

Uncertainties remain: exact 429 onset time relative to queue growth, whether other dependencies contributed, retry success baseline, the cost of elevated direct failures during retry suppression, and absence of deploy/schema/restart changes (E10) which excludes some causes but not misconfiguration of limits. A staged remediation is recommended: (1) cap/disable retries for throttled deps, (2) add circuit-breaking, (3) negotiate rate limits, (4) add per-dependency queue metrics, (5) load-test, (6) document runbook. Alternative hypothesis (internal resource exhaustion) is rejected because CPU/mem/disk stayed low (E04) and worker scaling barely helped (E07).","data":{"executive_summary":"Between 09:00 and 10:00 the DSH queue grew from 120 to 1,850 tasks while worker count held at 8 and resource utilization stayed low (CPU 43%, memory 51%, disk 22%).
